title: The Endless Cellar
premise: Folklorist Petra Nystrom arrives in the frost-bound village of Hällmark to record a harvest song that locals refuse to sing twice, lodging with the Vinter family, whose ancestral cellar holds something the household has fed for two hundred years. As mirrors begin lagging and the cellar's 'count' of names grows, Petra learns the family patriarch has been quietly adding outsiders to keep his own bloodline safe. Refusing to believe even as belief becomes survival, Petra must choose between exposing the family's crime to the village or leading them out ahead of the final count; she chooses escape, burning the songbook that binds them, though the last mirror still runs one second late.
about_author: Ada Pemberton is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing Scandinavian folk collections before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in the conviction that old songs remember what people prefer to forget.

chapters.title: The Song They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Petra Nystrom arrives in Hällmark by late bus, armed with recording equipment and cheerful skepticism. The Vinter family takes her in reluctantly; matriarch Signe warns her never to ask about the cellar door. At the tavern, an old man sings the harvest song once, then goes pale and leaves. Petra's POV establishes her rationalism and loneliness. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: House of Kept Things
chapters.summary: Settling into the Vinter house, Petra notices small wrongnesses: doors locked from outside, salt lines under thresholds, the youngest son Elias flinching at reflections. She records Signe humming fragments of the song, which sound different each time. From Elias's perspective we glimpse the family's dread. Emotional beat: the warmth of hospitality shadowed by rules no one will explain.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Petra catches it: her reflection in the hallway mirror moves a beat behind her. She blames fatigue, then tests every mirror in the house—each lags exactly one second, except those facing the cellar door, which show nothing at all. Her rationalism cracks for the first time. Emotional beat: denial curdling into fear as evidence refuses to stay deniable.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Counts
chapters.summary: Petra descends despite warnings and finds tally marks scratched into stone—hundreds of names, the newest dated weeks ago: a traveling salesman reported missing. Patriarch Henrik catches her there, and his calm menace reveals the family feeds the thing below a name each frost season. Emotional beat: horror of discovery compounded by realizing the family are perpetrators, not just victims.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Survival
chapters.summary: Henrik explains the covenant with bureaucratic tenderness: one name per winter, chosen from outsiders, keeps the village alive. Signe begs Petra to leave before the choosing. Petra, torn between fleeing and protecting Elias—who has confessed he was meant to be this year's name—stays. Emotional beat: love against duty, as Petra's attachment to Elias outweighs self-preservation.

chapters.title: Village of Complicit Bells
chapters.summary: Petra confronts the wider village and finds complicity everywhere: the priest blesses the choosing, the shopkeeper sells rope for the binding, everyone knows and no one speaks. Justice here exists entirely outside any law. A villager hints the song, sung fully twice, can unmake the covenant. Emotional beat: isolation deepening—the horror isn't hidden, it's municipal.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes Its Pattern
chapters.summary: First hard frost. Mirrors throughout the house now lag further, showing rooms as they were minutes ago—and in one, Petra sees herself writing in a ledger she's never touched. Henrik selects a name: not Elias, but Petra, having discovered her investigation. The family splits, some siding with Petra. Emotional beat: betrayal and the countdown made literal.

chapters.title: Sing It Twice
chapters.summary: Petra and Elias seek the old singer, who confesses he learned the song's second verse from his grandmother: sung twice in full, inside the house, it names the counter instead of the counted. But singing it requires someone willing to take the cellar's attention themselves. Petra records both verses, hands shaking. Emotional beat: resolve forged from terror—a weapon assembled from folklore.

chapters.title: The Count Reversed
chapters.summary: Climax. During the choosing rite, Petra plays and sings the song twice as Henrik drags her toward the cellar. The mirrors shatter outward; the lag reverses, reflections arriving before their owners. The cellar takes Henrik—the architect of the count—as its due, and the tally marks bleed away. Petra, Elias, and the defected family members flee the collapsing house. Emotional beat: terrible triumph at human cost.

chapters.title: After the Last Verse
chapters.summary: Resolution. In spring, Petra publishes nothing, burns her recordings, and leaves Hällmark with Elias. The village quietly resumes its silences; justice was done, but no law would recognize it. In a rest-stop bathroom mirror, Petra waves—and the reflection waves back one second late. She smiles anyway. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure, love chosen over safety, and the suggestion that some things follow you home.
